# How to use this guide

N-CHN(I)301 Child Health Nursing I is a Semester 5 subject of the INC 2021 B.Sc Nursing programme. It introduces the nursing care of children across the full age range from birth to adolescence — covering national policy, immunisation, hospital care, growth and development, neonatal care, the IMNCI framework, respiratory and endocrine diseases, and childhood emergencies. The companion subject N-CHN(II)301 (Semester 6) covers surgical, haematological, and other conditions and continues from this foundation.

## University examination pattern

Child Health Nursing I is examined in an end-semester written examination in Semester 5 of the INC 2021 programme:

| Section | Format | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Section A** | 20 multiple-choice questions × 1 mark | 20 |
| **Section B** | Attempt 2 out of 3 long essays × 10 marks | 20 |
| **Section C** | Attempt 7 out of 9 short answer questions × 5 marks | 35 |
| **Total** | | **75** |

Time: 3 hours. Confirm the exact pattern and internal choice structure with your university, as these may vary.

A separate **Quick MCQ test** (20 questions, 20 minutes) in this pack lets you drill facts quickly before class tests or viva.

## How the unit files map to the INC syllabus

The INC 2021 syllabus for N-CHN(I)301 has eight units. Each notes file covers one INC unit:

| Notes file | INC unit | Main topics covered |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit 1 | I | Modern concepts of child care, national child health programmes, child rights |
| Unit 2 | II | Preventive paediatrics, IYCF, growth monitoring, National Immunisation Schedule, cold chain, AEFI |
| Unit 3 | III | Hospitalised child, family-centred care, therapeutic play, paediatric nursing procedures |
| Unit 4 | IV | Growth, developmental milestones, developmental theories, nutrition, play, nutritional deficiencies |
| Unit 5 | V | Normal neonate (Apgar, immediate care), common neonatal conditions (jaundice, sepsis), preterm/LBW care, neonatal resuscitation |
| Unit 6 | VI | IMNCI: assessment framework, illness categories, classification, treatment, community workers |
| Unit 7 | VII | Respiratory diseases (croup, bronchiolitis, pneumonia, asthma, CF), endocrine diseases (CH, T1DM, GHD) |
| Unit 8 | VIII | Childhood emergencies: PAT, PBLS, febrile seizures, status epilepticus, septic shock, anaphylaxis, hypoglycaemia, DKA, drowning |

Study one notes file at a sitting. Read through the unit, then draw each `text` diagram once from memory. Attempt that unit's questions and MCQs without looking. Use the revision sheet for the night before the examination.

## Probability ratings

- **High** — a consistent favourite in INC B.Sc Nursing examinations; expect it in every paper in some form. Learn the full structured answer.
- **Medium** — appears in every other paper or as part of a larger question.
- **Low** — less frequent; still worth knowing for MCQs and very short answers.

These ratings are estimates based on the topic's weight in the INC syllabus and the emphasis placed on child health nursing in Indian nursing examinations. They are a guide, not a guarantee.

## High-probability topics by unit

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | National child health programmes (NHM/RCH, RBSK, ICDS), child rights, modern concepts |
| 2 | National Immunisation Schedule (table), cold chain (temperature, ILR, freeze-sensitive vaccines), AEFI (types, management, nurse's role) |
| 3 | Effects of hospitalisation by age (infant/toddler/school-age), family-centred care, Holliday-Segar fluid calculation, paediatric pain scales (FLACC, Faces, NRS) |
| 4 | Developmental milestones table (birth to 5 years), red flags for developmental delay, nutritional deficiency diseases (IDA, VAD, rickets, iodine) |
| 5 | Apgar score table, immediate care at birth, neonatal jaundice (physiological vs pathological, Kramer's zones, phototherapy nursing), birth asphyxia/NRP algorithm |
| 6 | IMNCI five steps, danger signs, fast breathing thresholds by age, dehydration plans A/B/C, SAM criteria |
| 7 | Croup vs epiglottitis comparison, asthma stepwise treatment, acute severe asthma management, congenital hypothyroidism (neonatal screening, features, treatment) |
| 8 | PBLS (differences from adult), febrile seizure management, DKA management (fluids over 48 h, insulin 0.1 U/kg/h), anaphylaxis (adrenaline IM dose) |

## Scoring tips for this subject

1. **Give the age-specific normal value.** An examiner asking about respiratory rate, heart rate, or blood glucose in a child expects the paediatric reference range, not the adult value. Cite units 4–8 normal values tables.

2. **Use the nursing care plan structure for clinical questions.** For any "nursing management of..." question, structure your answer as: Assessment → Nursing diagnoses → Planning → Implementation (medical management, nursing actions, health education) → Evaluation. This scores marks for organisation even if your clinical detail is not perfect.

3. **Answer comparison questions as a table.** Croup vs epiglottitis, physiological vs pathological jaundice, simple vs complex febrile seizure, IMNCI pink vs yellow vs green — tables are faster to write and easier to mark.

4. **Lead clinical answers with a definition.** One line before the main answer ("Febrile seizure is a seizure in a child aged 6 months to 5 years associated with fever > 38°C without evidence of intracranial infection or metabolic cause.") signals to the examiner that you understand the topic.

5. **State the IMNCI framework for sick-child questions.** When asked how to assess or manage a sick child under 5, mentioning IMNCI (assess, classify, treat/refer) shows integration of national guidelines and scores additional marks.

6. **Cite the National Immunisation Schedule accurately.** Examiners notice when students mix up ages, routes, and sites. Learn the schedule table in Unit 2 by heart.

7. **The night before**: read the "Remember" section at the end of each notes file; run the Quick MCQ test; review the revision sheet below.

# Last-night revision sheet — Child Health Nursing I

If you have one hour, work through this sheet in order: NIS table, milestones, Apgar, then emergency drug doses. Everything else can be read in 20 minutes.

---

## National Immunisation Schedule (abbreviated)

| Vaccine | Age | Route/site |
| --- | --- | --- |
| BCG, HepB (birth dose), OPV 0 | At birth | ID left arm / IM thigh / oral |
| Penta 1, OPV 1, RVV 1, PCV 1 | 6 weeks | IM thigh / oral / oral / IM thigh |
| Penta 2, OPV 2, RVV 2 | 10 weeks | IM thigh / oral / oral |
| Penta 3, OPV 3, RVV 3, PCV 2 | 14 weeks | IM thigh / oral / oral / IM thigh |
| Measles/MR 1, PCV booster, Vit A 1 lakh IU | 9 months | SC right arm / IM thigh / oral |
| DPT B1, MR 2, OPV booster, Vit A 2 lakh IU | 16–24 months | IM thigh / SC right arm / oral / oral |
| Vit A 2 lakh IU every 6 months | 18 months – 5 years | Oral |
| DPT Booster 2 | 5–6 years | IM deltoid |
| TT | 10 years, 16 years | IM deltoid |
| HPV (girls Class 6–9) | 2 doses, 0 and 6 months | IM deltoid |

**Freeze-sensitive** (must NEVER freeze): DPT, Penta, HepB, TT, PCV, RVV.  
**Cold chain**: 2–8°C; ILR = most reliable. VVM inner square darker than outer = discard.

---

## Growth — rules of thumb

| Measure | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Weight | Doubles at 5 months; trebles at 1 year; quadruples at 2 years |
| Height | Birth 50 cm; +25 cm at 1 year; +12.5 cm at 2 years; +5–6 cm/year |
| Head circumference | Birth 33–35 cm; 47 cm at 1 year; ~50 cm at 2 years |
| Anterior fontanelle | Closes 12–18 months |

---

## Developmental milestones — key ages (four domains)

| Age | Gross motor | Fine motor | Language | Social |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2 months | Head control (held steady) | Follows 180° | Cooing | **Social smile** |
| 6 months | Sits with support; rolls | Palmar grasp; transfers | Babbles | Stranger anxiety |
| 9 months | Sits alone; crawls | Inferior pincer | Dada/mama (non-specific) | Waves bye |
| 12 months | Stands; first steps | **Pincer grip** | 1–2 words | Separation anxiety peak |
| 18 months | Runs | Stacks 2–3 cubes | 10–20 words | Feeds self |
| 2 years | Runs well; stairs (2-feet/step) | Stacks 6; copies line | 2-word phrases | Parallel play |
| 3 years | Stands 1 foot 3 s; tricycle | Copies circle | Sentences; 300 words | Toilet trained day |
| 5 years | Skips | Copies triangle | Counts 10; knows colours | Dresses alone |

**Red flag**: regression (loss of an acquired skill) is ALWAYS abnormal.  
**Red flags**: not social smile by 3 m; not sitting by 9 m; not walking by 18 m; no speech by 18 m.

---

## Apgar score

| Sign | 0 | 1 | 2 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Appearance (colour) | Blue/pale all over | Blue extremities | Pink all over |
| Pulse | Absent | < 100/min | ≥ 100/min |
| Grimace (reflex) | None | Grimace | Cry/cough |
| Activity (tone) | Limp | Some flexion | Active |
| Respiration | Absent | Weak/irregular | Strong cry |

Score 7–10 normal; 4–6 moderate; 0–3 severe.

---

## Neonatal jaundice — key facts

| Feature | Physiological | Pathological |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Onset | > 24 hours | < 24 hours |
| Course | Peaks day 3–5; resolves by day 10–14 | Rising rapidly; persists |
| Causes | High RBC turnover, immature liver | Rh/ABO incompatibility, G6PD deficiency, sepsis |

**Phototherapy**: eye patches, unclothed, increase fluids 10–20%; monitor temperature.  
**Kramer Zone 5** (palms + soles yellow) = bilirubin > 15 mg/dL.

---

## Fast breathing thresholds (IMNCI)

| Age | Threshold |
| --- | --- |
| < 2 months | ≥ 60 /min |
| 2–12 months | ≥ 50 /min |
| 1–5 years | ≥ 40 /min |

---

## Dehydration plans (IMNCI/WHO)

| Plan | Degree | Treatment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | No dehydration | ORS at home 50–100 mL after each loose stool; continue breastfeeding |
| B | Some dehydration | 75 mL/kg ORS over 4 hours in facility; zinc 20 mg/day × 10 days |
| C | Severe dehydration | Ringer's lactate 100 mL/kg IV (30 mL/kg fast, then 70 mL/kg slower) |

---

## SAM / MAM criteria

| Category | MUAC | W/H Z-score | Oedema |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SAM (refer) | < 11.5 cm | < −3 | Bilateral pitting |
| MAM (treat) | 11.5–12.5 cm | −2 to −3 | None |

---

## Paediatric BLS (PBLS) — key differences from adult

| Point | PBLS | Adult BLS |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Initial breaths | **5** rescue breaths | 2 rescue breaths |
| Compression:ventilation ratio | **15:2** (2 rescuers); 30:2 (1 rescuer) | 30:2 |
| Compression depth | **1/3 chest AP** (~4 cm infant, ~5 cm child) | 5–6 cm |
| Compression rate | 100–120/min | 100–120/min |
| Infant technique | 2-thumb encircling | — |
| AED | From **1 year** (paediatric pads) | Any age |

---

## Emergency drug doses

| Drug | Indication | Dose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Adrenaline (cardiac arrest) | HR < 60 despite CPR | 0.01 mg/kg IV/IO; 0.1 mg/kg ETT |
| Adrenaline (anaphylaxis) | Anaphylaxis | 0.01 mg/kg IM anterolateral thigh (max 0.5 mg) |
| Dextrose 10% | Hypoglycaemia | 2 mL/kg IV bolus over 5 min |
| Diazepam PR | Febrile/acute seizure > 5 min | 0.5 mg/kg PR |
| Midazolam buccal | Febrile/acute seizure > 5 min | 0.2–0.3 mg/kg |
| Lorazepam IV | Status epilepticus (1st line) | 0.1 mg/kg IV |
| Phenytoin IV | Status epilepticus (2nd line) | 20 mg/kg IV over 20 min (ECG monitor) |
| IV fluid (shock) | Septic shock, severe dehydration | 20 mL/kg 0.9% NaCl bolus; reassess |

---

## DKA — key management points

1. IV fluids (0.9% NaCl or Ringer's lactate) corrected over **48 hours** (not fast — cerebral oedema risk).
2. Insulin infusion 0.05–0.1 U/kg/h — start **1–2 hours after fluids**.
3. Potassium replacement once urine output confirmed.
4. Monitor neurological status hourly — headache/change in consciousness = cerebral oedema → mannitol 0.25–1 g/kg IV.

---

## Nutritional deficiencies — one-liners

| Deficiency | Key sign | Treatment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| IDA (Hb < 11) | Pallor, pica, koilonychia | Ferrous sulfate 3–6 mg/kg/day × 3 months |
| Vitamin A | Night blindness → Bitot's spots → keratomalacia | Mega-dose at 9 months (1 lakh IU), then 2 lakh IU/6 months |
| Iodine | Goitre; cretinism (maternal deficiency) | Iodised salt |
| Vitamin D rickets | Bow legs, Harrison's sulcus, craniotabes | Vitamin D 1,500–5,000 IU/day + calcium |

---

**Exam reminder**: 75-mark paper, 3 hours. Write paediatric normal values (not adult values). Use IMNCI framework for sick child ≤ 5 years. Structure clinical answers as Assessment → Nursing care → Health education. Comparison tables score marks quickly.

# Unit 1: Modern concepts of child-care; national policy, programmes and child rights

This unit is the first part of INC Unit I. It explains what "child health" means today, how child-care has changed over time, the national and international framework that protects children, the main welfare programmes in India, and how we measure the health of children with morbidity and mortality rates. These are the ideas every later unit builds on.

## 1.1 Who is a "child"? Some common terms

| Term | Age |
| --- | --- |
| Neonate (newborn) | Birth to 28 days |
| Infant | Birth to 1 year |
| Toddler | 1 to 3 years |
| Pre-school child | 3 to 6 years |
| School-age child | 6 to 12 years |
| Adolescent | 10 to 19 years (WHO) |
| Under-five | Birth to below 5 years |

**Paediatrics** is the branch of medicine dealing with children; **child health nursing** is the care of children in health and illness, with the family at the centre.

## 1.2 Historical development of child health

- In early times child-care was a purely family and religious matter; sickness and death in childhood were accepted as fate, and infant death was very common.
- Organised child health began with the recognition that most childhood deaths are **preventable** — from infection, poor feeding and unsafe birth.
- Milestones in the modern era: the founding of child welfare societies, maternal and child health (MCH) clinics, the start of **immunization**, the spread of **oral rehydration therapy (ORT)** for diarrhoea, and the worldwide push to control vaccine-preventable diseases.
- In India, child health moved from scattered charity to a planned, government-led service through the Five-Year Plans, the primary health centre (PHC) network, the **Reproductive and Child Health** programme, and today's National Health Mission.

## 1.3 Philosophy and modern concept of child-care

The modern approach can be summed up in a few principles:

- **The child is not a small adult.** Children differ in body, mind and needs, so care, drug amounts and communication must suit the age.
- **Family-centred care.** The family is the constant in a child's life; parents are partners in care, not visitors. Care supports the whole family.
- **Atraumatic care.** Reduce the physical and emotional distress of illness and treatment — prevent or minimise separation, pain and fear.
- **Growth and development focus.** Every contact is a chance to promote normal growth, development and good habits, not only to treat disease.
- **Prevention first.** Promotion of health and prevention of disease (immunization, nutrition, safe environment) come before cure.
- **Rights-based and holistic.** The child has rights; care covers physical, emotional, social and spiritual needs.

**Changing trends** in child-care: a shift from hospital cure to community prevention and promotion; shorter hospital stays and more day-care and home-based care; parents staying with the child; play and school continued during illness; team care; and strong national programmes reaching the village through the ASHA and Anganwadi worker.

## 1.4 Cultural and religious considerations in child-care

Beliefs and customs strongly shape how families feed, name, protect and treat their children. A nurse must learn the family's practices and work with them.

- **Feeding customs:** when breastfeeding is started, whether **colostrum** is given or discarded, "hot" and "cold" food beliefs, prelacteal feeds (honey, water, ghutti). The nurse gently corrects harmful practices (discarding colostrum, early water) while respecting helpful ones.
- **Naming and birth rituals**, head-shaving, ear-piercing, applying kajal, threads and amulets.
- **Illness beliefs:** some families first seek traditional or faith healers; the nurse keeps a non-judgemental manner and guides the family to safe, timely care.
- **Religious needs** around diet, prayer, and care of the dying child must be respected.

Culturally sensitive care builds trust and improves follow-up and immunization.

## 1.5 National policy and legislation for child health and welfare

India protects children through policy and law:

- **National Health Policy 2017** — aims to raise life expectancy, lower infant and under-five mortality, achieve universal immunization and strengthen primary care.
- **National Policy for Children (2013)** — declares every person below 18 a child and lists survival, health, nutrition, education, development and protection as priorities.
- **The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009** — free, compulsory education for children aged 6–14 years.
- **Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015** — care, protection and rehabilitation of children in need and children in conflict with law.
- **Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012** — protects children from sexual abuse and exploitation.
- **Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act** — prohibits employment of children below 14 years.
- **Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006**, the **PC-PNDT Act** (bans sex determination to prevent female foeticide), and the **Infant Milk Substitutes (IMS) Act** (restricts advertising of breast-milk substitutes and protects breastfeeding).

> Laws are updated from time to time; confirm the current title and provisions before using them in practice.

## 1.6 National programmes and agencies for child welfare

| Programme / agency | Main purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) | Through the **Anganwadi centre**: supplementary nutrition, pre-school education, immunization, health check-up, referral and nutrition/health education for children under 6 and mothers |
| Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child, Adolescent Health (RMNCH+A) | The umbrella strategy linking care across the life stages |
| Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK) | Child health screening for the **4 D's — Defects at birth, Diseases, Deficiencies, and Development delays/disabilities** — with free treatment |
| Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram (RKSK) | Adolescent health |
| Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY) & Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK) | Promote safe institutional delivery and free care for mother and sick newborn/child |
| Home-Based Newborn Care (HBNC) & Facility-Based Newborn Care (FBNC) | ASHA home visits to newborns; sick newborn care units (SNCU), newborn stabilisation and care corners |
| Universal Immunization Programme (UIP) & Mission Indradhanush | Free vaccines to all children and pregnant women (covered in Unit 2) |
| POSHAN Abhiyaan | National nutrition mission to reduce stunting, wasting, anaemia and low birth weight |

**Agencies:** WHO and **UNICEF** (United Nations Children's Fund) support programmes worldwide; in India, the Indian Academy of Pediatrics (IAP), the Indian Council for Child Welfare, and state health departments deliver services; the ASHA, ANM and Anganwadi worker are the front-line team.

## 1.7 Internationally accepted rights of the child

The **United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC, 1989)** is the main international charter; India ratified it in 1992. Its rights are grouped into four:

- **Survival** — life, health, nutrition, a name and nationality.
- **Development** — education, play, leisure, and freedom of thought.
- **Protection** — from abuse, neglect, exploitation, child labour and harmful work.
- **Participation** — the right to be heard and to express views on matters affecting the child.

The guiding idea is the **best interests of the child**.

## 1.8 Changing trends in hospital, preventive, promotive and curative care

| Aspect | Older approach | Modern approach |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Where care happens | Mostly in hospital | Community and home, with hospital for the seriously ill |
| Family | Kept away | Stays with the child; a partner in care |
| Focus | Cure of disease | Prevention and promotion first, then cure |
| Procedures | Routine, often distressing | Atraumatic; play, preparation and pain control |
| Record and follow-up | Paper, clinic-based | Growth charts, immunization cards, digital records, home follow-up by ASHA |

## 1.9 Differences between an adult and a child that affect the response to illness

A child reacts to illness differently from an adult. The nurse must keep these differences in mind.

| Area | How the child differs |
| --- | --- |
| **Physiological** | Larger body-surface-area to weight ratio → faster heat and fluid loss; higher metabolic rate and fluid turnover → dehydrates quickly; smaller, softer airway → blocks easily; immature liver and kidneys → handle drugs differently; faster heart and breathing rates; bones are growing |
| **Psychological** | Depends on parents; cannot express feelings in words; shows **separation anxiety** (especially 6 months–3 years); has **magical thinking** and fears (of the dark, of procedures, of mutilation); may see illness as punishment |
| **Social** | The whole family is affected; illness disrupts school and play; the child needs the family present |
| **Immunological** | Immature immune system; passive immunity from the mother wanes by a few months; so the young child catches infections easily and needs immunization |

These differences explain why children fall ill fast, deteriorate quickly, but also recover quickly with the right early care.

## 1.10 Child morbidity and mortality rates

Rates let us measure and compare the health of children and plan services.

| Rate | What it counts (per 1000) |
| --- | --- |
| **Neonatal mortality rate (NMR)** | Deaths of infants in the first 28 days, per 1000 live births |
| **Infant mortality rate (IMR)** | Deaths of infants below 1 year, per 1000 live births |
| **Under-five (child) mortality rate (U5MR)** | Deaths of children below 5 years, per 1000 live births |
| **Perinatal mortality rate** | Stillbirths plus deaths in the first week, per 1000 total births |
| **Maternal mortality ratio (MMR)** | Maternal deaths per 100,000 live births |
| **Morbidity** | How much illness there is in the child population (incidence and prevalence of disease) |

- **IMR is the most sensitive index of a country's health and living standards.** India's IMR, NMR and U5MR have fallen steadily over the years. Confirm the latest figures from the **Sample Registration System (SRS)** and **National Family Health Survey (NFHS)**, as they change each year.
- **Leading causes of under-five death** in India: prematurity and low birth weight, birth asphyxia, **pneumonia**, **diarrhoea**, neonatal infections (sepsis), and congenital anomalies. Most are preventable — which is why prevention, immunization, breastfeeding and early treatment are the heart of this subject.

## 1.11 Application and implication in nursing

- Treat the family as partner and the child as a growing person, not a small adult.
- Learn and respect the family's culture; correct only the harmful practices, and do so gently.
- Know the national programmes so you can refer families to ICDS, RBSK, JSY/JSSK and immunization services.
- Use rights-based, atraumatic, family-centred care in every contact.
- Understand the rates so you can read district data, find high-risk groups and explain to families why prevention matters.

## Remember

- The child is not a small adult: body, mind and needs differ.
- Modern care = family-centred + atraumatic + prevention-first + rights-based.
- Age terms: neonate <28 days, infant <1 yr, toddler 1–3, pre-school 3–6, school-age 6–12.
- CRC 1989, India ratified 1992: survival, development, protection, participation; best interests of the child.
- RBSK screens the **4 D's**: Defects at birth, Diseases, Deficiencies, Development delays/disabilities.
- ICDS works through the **Anganwadi centre**; ASHA gives Home-Based Newborn Care.
- IMR = deaths below 1 year per 1000 live births; **most sensitive index of health status**. NMR <28 days; U5MR <5 years.
- Top under-five killers: prematurity/LBW, birth asphyxia, pneumonia, diarrhoea, neonatal sepsis — nearly all preventable.
- Separation anxiety is strongest between about 6 months and 3 years.

# Unit 2: Preventive paediatrics and immunization

This unit covers INC Unit II: levels of prevention in child health, national programmes for child welfare, the National Immunisation Schedule, cold chain management, and adverse events following immunisation. Immunisation is one of the highest-probability examination topics in this subject.

---

## 2.1 Levels of prevention in child health

Prevention is classified into three levels. The goal in paediatrics is to shift every child from the later levels back to primary prevention.

| Level | Aim | Examples in child health |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Primary prevention** | Stop disease before it starts | Immunisation, exclusive breastfeeding, safe water and sanitation, vitamin A supplementation, iodised salt |
| **Secondary prevention** | Early detection and prompt treatment | Newborn screening (TSH for congenital hypothyroidism, G6PD), growth monitoring with WHO charts, IMNCI assessment, vision screening |
| **Tertiary prevention** | Limit disability and rehabilitate | Early intervention for developmental delay, special education, physiotherapy for cerebral palsy, corrective surgery for cleft palate |

**Primary prevention is always cheaper and more effective than treatment.** Nurses spend most of their child health work at this level.

## 2.2 Infant and young child feeding (IYCF)

Malnutrition in India is closely linked to poor feeding practices. WHO and UNICEF IYCF recommendations:

- **Exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months** — only breast milk; no water, no other milk, no food.
- **Initiate breastfeeding within one hour of birth** — the first milk (colostrum) is rich in antibodies (secretory IgA) and must not be discarded.
- **Complementary feeding from 6 months** — introduce semi-solid foods while continuing breastfeeding; start with soft mashes, gradually increase texture.
- **Continue breastfeeding up to 2 years or beyond.**

No infant formula substitutes for the immunological factors in breast milk: secretory IgA, lactoferrin, lysozyme, macrophages, and T-lymphocytes. Formula-fed infants have higher rates of diarrhoea, respiratory infection, and otitis media.

## 2.3 Growth monitoring

**Growth is the best single indicator of child health and nutrition.**

- Measure weight, length/height, and head circumference at every visit and plot on a WHO Child Growth Standards chart.
- WHO charts use **Z-scores** (standard deviations from the median):

| Z-score | Nutritional status |
| --- | --- |
| Above +2 | Overweight (weight-for-height) |
| −1 to +2 | Normal |
| Below −2 | Underweight (or wasted/stunted) |
| Below −3 | Severely underweight |

- **Gomez classification** (weight-for-age): Grade I 76–90% of median (mild); Grade II 61–75% (moderate); Grade III ≤60% (severe).
- **MUAC (mid-upper arm circumference)**: quick screening tool for SAM — MUAC < 11.5 cm = severe acute malnutrition; 11.5–12.5 cm = moderate acute malnutrition (MAM).

**Nurse's role**: weigh the child accurately (remove clothes, calibrate scales), plot on the chart, recognise faltering growth, counsel the mother on feeding, refer SAM/MAM as needed.

## 2.4 IMNCI overview

**Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI)** is a WHO/UNICEF strategy integrated into India's National Health Mission to reduce child mortality.

- **Target age**: 0–59 months (young infant chart 0–2 months; child chart 2–59 months).
- **Integrated approach**: a single child health worker (ASHA, ANM, or nurse) assesses all major causes of child death (ARI, diarrhoea, malaria, measles, malnutrition, anaemia) in one visit rather than by organ system.
- **Simplified guidelines**: only the signs needed to identify children requiring referral, specific treatment, or home care — not a full clinical examination.

**The IMNCI five steps for the sick child (2–59 months):**

```text
ASK → CHECK → CLASSIFY → IDENTIFY TREATMENT → TREAT / REFER / COUNSEL / FOLLOW-UP
```

**Danger signs** — refer any child with even one:
- Cannot drink or breastfeed
- Vomits everything
- Convulsions (now or in the last illness)
- Lethargic or unconscious
- Severe malnutrition with oedema

**Colour coding of classification**:
- **Pink**: urgent referral to hospital
- **Yellow**: specific treatment at clinic (antibiotics, ORS, zinc)
- **Green**: home treatment and counselling

**Role of community workers**: ASHA counsels on IYCF, identifies sick children and refers, records births and deaths. AWW (anganwadi worker) provides nutrition supplementation under ICDS, monitors growth, identifies SAM.

## 2.5 National child health programmes

### National Health Mission (NHM)

The NHM merges the NRHM (rural) and NUHM (urban) missions. Its Reproductive and Child Health (RCH) component covers:
- Antenatal care, skilled birth attendance, postnatal visits.
- Child immunisation (Universal Immunisation Programme — UIP).
- IMNCI.
- FBNC (Facility Based Newborn Care) — at health centres for sick neonates.
- HBNC (Home Based Newborn Care) — ASHAs make 7 home visits in the first 42 days.

### RBSK — Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram

Screens children 0–18 years for the **4 Ds**:
1. **Defects at birth** (congenital hypothyroidism, CHD, cleft lip/palate, neural tube defects)
2. **Diseases** (anaemia, dental caries, skin conditions, ear infections)
3. **Deficiencies** (vitamin D, iron, iodine)
4. **Developmental delays and disabilities** (vision, hearing, locomotor, learning, autism, cerebral palsy)

Mobile Health Teams (medical officer + 2 RBSK health workers) screen children at anganwadis and government schools.

### ICDS — Integrated Child Development Services

Targets children under 6 and pregnant/lactating women. Provides **six services**:
1. Supplementary nutrition (take-home rations)
2. Immunisation (through the AWW/ANM link)
3. Health check-up
4. Referral services
5. Pre-school education (3–6 years)
6. Nutrition and health education to mothers

### Mid-Day Meal Scheme

Hot cooked meal to children in government schools; reduces dropout, improves nutrition status, especially protein-energy malnutrition and iron-deficiency anaemia.

### POSHAN Abhiyaan (National Nutrition Mission)

India's flagship multi-ministry programme to reduce stunting, undernutrition, anaemia and low birth weight. Uses a technology-based real-time monitoring system; targets are measured against baseline.

## 2.6 Immunisation — the National Immunisation Schedule

India's Universal Immunisation Programme (UIP) provides free vaccines to all children. The current schedule is:

| Vaccine | Age | Route | Site | Dose |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| BCG | At birth | Intradermal | Left upper arm | 0.1 mL (>1 month: 0.05 mL) |
| Hepatitis B (1st) | At birth | Intramuscular | Anterolateral thigh | 0.5 mL |
| OPV (0 dose) | At birth | Oral | Mouth | 2 drops |
| OPV 1 | 6 weeks | Oral | Mouth | 2 drops |
| OPV 2 | 10 weeks | Oral | Mouth | 2 drops |
| OPV 3 | 14 weeks | Oral | Mouth | 2 drops |
| Penta 1 (DPT+HepB+Hib) | 6 weeks | Intramuscular | Anterolateral thigh | 0.5 mL |
| Penta 2 | 10 weeks | Intramuscular | Anterolateral thigh | 0.5 mL |
| Penta 3 | 14 weeks | Intramuscular | Anterolateral thigh | 0.5 mL |
| Rotavirus vaccine (RVV) 1 | 6 weeks | Oral | Mouth | 5 drops |
| RVV 2 | 10 weeks | Oral | Mouth | 5 drops |
| RVV 3 | 14 weeks | Oral | Mouth | 5 drops |
| PCV 1 (Pneumococcal) | 6 weeks | Intramuscular | Anterolateral thigh | 0.5 mL |
| PCV 2 | 14 weeks | Intramuscular | Anterolateral thigh | 0.5 mL |
| PCV Booster | 9 months | Intramuscular | Anterolateral thigh | 0.5 mL |
| Measles/MR 1 | 9–12 months | Subcutaneous | Right upper arm | 0.5 mL |
| Vitamin A (1st) | 9 months | Oral | — | 1 lakh IU |
| DPT Booster 1 | 16–24 months | Intramuscular | Anterolateral thigh | 0.5 mL |
| Measles/MR 2 | 16–24 months | Subcutaneous | Right upper arm | 0.5 mL |
| OPV Booster | 16–24 months | Oral | Mouth | 2 drops |
| Vitamin A (2nd–9th) | Every 6 months (18 months–5 years) | Oral | — | 2 lakh IU |
| DPT Booster 2 | 5–6 years | Intramuscular | Deltoid | 0.5 mL |
| TT | 10 years, 16 years | Intramuscular | Deltoid | 0.5 mL |
| JE (selected districts) | 9 months (1st), 16–24 months (2nd) | Subcutaneous | Right upper arm | 0.5 mL |
| HPV (girls, Class 6–9) | 2 doses (0 and 6 months) | Intramuscular | Deltoid | 0.5 mL |

**Note**: Confirm the current schedule with the Ministry of Health; it is updated periodically.

## 2.7 Cold chain

Vaccines are biological products destroyed by heat or freezing. The cold chain is the system of refrigerated storage and transport from manufacturer to child.

**Temperature requirement**: most vaccines must be kept at **+2°C to +8°C**.

**Key equipment**:
- **Walk-in cold rooms** at national/state stores (−15° to −25°C for OPV)
- **Ice-lined refrigerators (ILR)** at district/PHC level — liner of ice keeps vaccines cold even during power failure; most reliable piece of equipment
- **Deep freezers** for OPV (−15° to −25°C)
- **Cold boxes** for transport between stores
- **Vaccine carriers** for outreach sessions

**Freeze-sensitive vaccines** — must NEVER freeze: DPT, Penta, Hep B, TT, PCV, RVV. Freezing destroys them and makes them look normal. Use the **shake test** to detect frozen-and-thawed DPT/Penta/HepB (frozen vials clump and do not re-disperse). Use **Freeze Watch indicators** in cold boxes.

**Vaccine Vial Monitors (VVM)**: a heat-sensitive label on each vial. As cumulative heat exposure rises, the inner square darkens. Do not use the vaccine if the inner square is as dark as or darker than the outer circle.

**Nurse's role in cold chain**: check temperatures twice daily, record in a register, never put food or drinks in a vaccine refrigerator, place vaccines according to their cold-chain requirement (OPV at the top/freezer, freeze-sensitive at the bottom/away from freezing coils), do not put vaccines in the door (temperature fluctuates most there).

## 2.8 Adverse events following immunisation (AEFI)

An **AEFI** is any untoward medical event that follows immunisation. It may or may not be caused by the vaccine.

### Classification

| Type | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Vaccine-induced** | Caused by the vaccine's inherent properties | BCG abscess, OPV-associated paralytic poliomyelitis (rare) |
| **Programme error** | Caused by errors in preparation/handling/administration | Abscess from non-sterile technique, wrong dose, wrong vaccine |
| **Injection-related** | Caused by the injection act, not the vaccine | Fainting, local pain, nerve injury |
| **Coincidental** | Would have happened anyway; not caused by vaccine | Fever from another infection on the same day |
| **Unknown** | Cannot be classified | — |

### Common AEFIs

- **Local**: redness, swelling, tenderness at the site — most common; manage with cold compress.
- **BCG**: small ulcer at the injection site (normal reaction); BCG lymphadenitis (enlarged, sometimes suppurating axillary lymph node) — refer to district for management.
- **DPT/Penta**: fever, local swelling, irritability — reassure parents; paracetamol for fever.
- **OPV**: very rarely vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis (VAPP) — 1 in ~2.5 million doses.
- **MMR/Measles**: fever 7–10 days after vaccination, mild rash — normal.
- **Febrile seizures**: can follow fever from any vaccine, most commonly DTwP — reassure parents that most are self-limiting.
- **Anaphylaxis** (very rare): within minutes; bronchospasm, urticaria, collapse — keep adrenaline 1:1000 available; give 0.01 mL/kg IM immediately, call for help.

### Nurse's role

1. Record all AEFIs in the immunisation register and on the AEFI form.
2. Manage local reactions (cold compress, paracetamol for fever).
3. Manage anaphylaxis immediately.
4. Report serious AEFIs (hospitalisation, death, cluster) to the district immunisation officer within 24 hours.
5. Counsel parents that mild reactions (pain, fever) are normal and expected.

### Contraindications

- **True contraindications to live vaccines** (OPV, measles/MR, BCG, JE): severe immunodeficiency (chemotherapy, congenital immune defects), **except** HIV-positive children who are asymptomatic or on ART with adequate immune status (BCG and measles may be given).
- **High fever** on the day of vaccination — defer and revisit; mild illness (cough, cold) is NOT a contraindication.
- **Previous anaphylaxis** to a specific vaccine component — do not repeat that vaccine.
- Malnutrition is NOT a contraindication; malnourished children need vaccines more.

### Catch-up immunisation

If a child missed one or more doses, do not restart from zero. Continue from where it was left off, leaving the minimum interval between doses (usually 4 weeks for primary series). The nurse's role: identify missed children from registers, do outreach sessions to reach them.

## Remember

- Primary prevention (immunisation, breastfeeding) is cheaper and more effective than treatment.
- IYCF: exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months; complementary feeding from 6 months; breastfeeding until 2 years.
- MUAC < 11.5 cm = SAM; 11.5–12.5 cm = MAM.
- National Immunisation Schedule: BCG, OPV, Penta, PCV, RVV at 6–10–14 weeks; MR at 9 months; boosters at 16–24 months; HPV for girls Class 6–9.
- Cold chain: 2–8°C; ILR is the most reliable piece; freeze-sensitive vaccines (DPT, Penta, HepB, TT) must never freeze.
- VVM: inner square darker than outer circle = discard vaccine.
- AEFI: record, manage, report within 24 hours if serious; keep adrenaline ready for anaphylaxis.
- Malnutrition is NOT a contraindication to immunisation.
- RBSK screens for 4 Ds; ICDS provides 6 services; POSHAN Abhiyaan targets stunting, undernutrition, anaemia.

# Unit 3: The hospitalised child and child health nursing procedures

This unit covers INC Unit III: the effects of hospitalisation on children and families, family-centred care, therapeutic play, and the key nursing procedures performed in paediatric settings. Understanding the developmental impact of hospitalisation helps the nurse plan care that reduces distress.

---

## 3.1 Effects of hospitalisation on children

Children experience hospitalisation differently depending on their developmental stage.

| Age group | Main fears | Behavioural responses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Infant (0–12 months)** | Separation from parent, pain, strange environment | Crying, feeding difficulties, regression in development |
| **Toddler (1–3 years)** | Most severely affected; separation anxiety, loss of control | Protest (crying loudly, reaching for parent), Despair (withdrawn, quiet crying), Detachment (appears adjusted but has emotionally withdrawn) |
| **Preschool (3–6 years)** | Fear of body mutilation, guilt (thinks illness is punishment), magical thinking | Regression (bedwetting, thumb-sucking), aggression, withdrawal |
| **School-age (6–12 years)** | Loss of control, boredom, fear of death, peer separation | Cooperation with procedures but worries about missing school and friends; asks detailed questions |
| **Adolescent (12–18 years)** | Threat to identity and body image, separation from peers, loss of independence | Anger, non-compliance, withdrawal; concerned about appearance |

**Robertson's three phases** of separation response in toddlers:
1. **Protest** — loud crying, calling for the parent, cannot be comforted.
2. **Despair** — quiet, withdrawn, still grieving but appearing calmer; nurses may mistake this for acceptance.
3. **Detachment** — appears settled, interacts, but has emotionally distanced from the parent; most harmful phase.

### Effects on the family

- **Parents**: anxiety, guilt, fear, disrupted work and finances; they may feel helpless and blame themselves.
- **Siblings**: jealousy, rivalry, feeling ignored; may show behavioural or school problems.
- **Financial stress**: parents in India often face substantial out-of-pocket expenses even in public hospitals; job loss from hospital stays is common.

## 3.2 Minimising the stress of hospitalisation

### Family-centred care

The philosophy that the family is the constant in the child's life and that the healthcare system must support and partner with families. Key elements:
- Parents are welcome 24 hours a day (**rooming-in**); a parent's presence is the single most effective way to reduce separation anxiety.
- Parents participate in direct care (feeding, bathing, comforting) — teach them rather than taking over.
- Respect cultural and family values in care decisions.
- Treat parents as partners, give them honest, clear information.

### Preparation for procedures

- Use **age-appropriate language** — say "it will feel like a pinch" not "this won't hurt."
- Give **honest, brief explanations** just before the procedure, not hours ahead (which creates anxiety in young children).
- Allow the child to handle equipment if safe.
- Use **therapeutic play** — let the child role-play procedures on a doll.
- Allow the **parent to be present** during most procedures; evidence shows it reduces distress for both child and parent.

### Maintaining routine

Keeping mealtimes, nap times, and familiar objects (a favourite toy or blanket — a "transitional object") reduces disorientation.

### Comfort positions

- **Side-lying with knees drawn up**: for lumbar puncture.
- **Upright on parent's lap with arms wrapped**: for IV insertion in young children (less frightening than being held down on the bed).
- **Semi-prone**: for children with breathing difficulty.
- Never physically restrain a child unless essential and only for the minimum time needed.

## 3.3 Play in hospital

**Play is the work of childhood** — it promotes development even during illness.

| Type | Description | Hospital use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Developmental play** | Age-appropriate activities for normal growth | Art, puzzles, books, games brought from home |
| **Therapeutic play** | Planned play to help child cope with hospitalisation | Medical play (syringes without needles, bandaging a doll), puppet play to express fears |
| **Distraction play** | Used during procedures | Blowing bubbles, music, holding a favourite toy |

A **play specialist/child life specialist** may be available in larger hospitals; the nurse initiates basic therapeutic play when this specialist is not available.

## 3.4 Medication administration in children

### Principles

- Always use **weight-based dosing** (mg/kg); calculate carefully.
- Double-check calculations for all IV medications.
- Explain the procedure to the child and parent.

### Routes

**Oral**:
- Use an oral syringe (not a household spoon) for accuracy.
- Mix crushed tablets or liquid in a small amount of food or juice — but not in the full feeding (the child may not finish it).
- Avoid masking taste with essential foods; children may then refuse that food.

**Intramuscular (IM)**:
- **Vastus lateralis** (outer middle third of the thigh) is the preferred site in infants and toddlers (largest muscle mass; no major nerves or vessels).
- **Deltoid** may be used in older children (≥3 years) for small volumes.
- Use the smallest-gauge needle adequate; use EMLA cream or cold spray beforehand when available.

**Intravenous (IV)**:
- Calculate the volume and rate carefully: use a volume-control burette (Buretrol/Metriset) to prevent accidental fluid overload.
- Rate: prescribed as mL/hour; for microdrip sets (60 drops/mL), drip rate = mL/h.
- **Smart pumps** (syringe drivers and infusion pumps) are preferred for accuracy and safety.
- Monitor hourly for extravasation (swelling, blanching, pain around the site) — especially important in neonates and infants.
- In infants when no peripheral vein is accessible: **scalp veins** (superficial temporal, frontal, occipital) may be used; explain to parents that shaving is temporary.

## 3.5 Intravenous access

| Access type | Use | Nurse's role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Peripheral IV cannula** | Short-term IV therapy | Insert at peripheral site (back of hand, antecubital fossa, foot, scalp vein in infants); check every hour for infiltration, phlebitis |
| **Umbilical venous catheter (UVC)** | Neonates in first few days | Inserted by doctor; nurse monitors position, secures, prevents disconnection |
| **PICC (peripherally inserted central catheter)** | Long-term antibiotics, TPN | Inserted under ultrasound guidance; nurse maintains dressing, monitors for infection |
| **Central venous line** | Critical illness, chemotherapy | Doctor inserts; nurse monitors all connections, keeps sterile dressing |

## 3.6 Fluid and electrolyte management

### Holliday-Segar formula for daily maintenance fluids

| Weight | Daily requirement |
| --- | --- |
| First 10 kg | 100 mL/kg/day |
| Next 10 kg (10–20 kg) | 50 mL/kg/day |
| Each kg above 20 kg | 20 mL/kg/day |

**Example**: a 25 kg child needs (10 × 100) + (10 × 50) + (5 × 20) = 1000 + 500 + 100 = **1600 mL/day** = 67 mL/hour.

### Dehydration assessment

| Feature | Mild (<5%) | Moderate (5–10%) | Severe (>10%) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Alertness | Normal | Irritable | Lethargic/unconscious |
| Eyes | Normal | Sunken | Very sunken |
| Skin turgor | Normal | Goes back slowly (>2 s) | Goes back very slowly (>3 s) |
| Mouth/tongue | Moist | Dry | Very dry, parched |
| Tears | Present | Decreased | Absent |
| Capillary refill | <2 s | 2–3 s | >3 s |
| Urine output | Normal | Reduced | Very reduced or absent |

**ORS (Oral Rehydration Solution)**: WHO/UNICEF low-osmolarity ORS (Na 75 mEq/L, glucose 75 mmol/L). Zinc supplement 20 mg/day for 10 days with every episode of diarrhoea reduces duration and severity.

**IMNCI fluid plans**:
- **Plan A** (no dehydration): give ORS at home, 50–100 mL after each loose stool; continue breastfeeding.
- **Plan B** (some dehydration): give 75 mL/kg of ORS over 4 hours in the facility; reassess after 4 hours.
- **Plan C** (severe dehydration): IV Ringer's lactate 100 mL/kg (30 mL/kg fast in 30 min for infants, then 70 mL/kg over 2.5 h; for older children 30 mL/kg fast then 70 mL/kg over 2.5 h).

## 3.7 Nasogastric tube feeding

**Indications**: unable to feed orally, prematurity, respiratory distress, post-operative feeding.

**Tube size**: 5 Fr neonates; 6–8 Fr infants; 10–12 Fr older children.

**Placement check**:
- Measure from tip of nose to ear to xiphoid process to determine insertion length; mark and insert.
- Confirm placement: aspirate gastric contents (pH should be <5.5); X-ray is gold standard if in doubt; never rely only on auscultation.
- Secure with hypoallergenic tape; document the external length.

**Feeding**: bolus (over 20–30 min by gravity) is more physiological; continuous pump feeding for premature infants or those with high aspiration risk.

**Checking residuals**: aspirate before each bolus; if residual > half the last feed volume, hold feeding and re-assess.

**Parental education for home NG**: teach placement check, gravity feeding, flushing with clean water, signs of displacement (coughing, choking, change in colour).

## 3.8 Paediatric blood transfusion

- Volume: **10–15 mL/kg** of packed red cells raises Hb by approximately 2–3 g/dL.
- Pre-transfusion: check patient identity, blood group and cross-match certificate, blood bag label for expiry and appearance; take baseline vital signs.
- Infuse slowly for first 15 minutes; monitor closely; complete within 4 hours.
- Monitor for transfusion reactions: fever, chills, urticaria, back pain, haemoglobinuria — stop immediately, keep IV line open with saline, inform doctor.

## 3.9 Restraints

Restraints are used only when essential to protect the child during a procedure, never as routine.

- **Mummy (papoose) restraint**: wrap the child snugly in a sheet to restrain arms and legs for procedures on the head/neck.
- **Elbow restraint**: keeps the elbow straight (prevents the child from bending and touching a scalp IV or face wound).
- **Documentation**: type, time applied, time removed, skin condition checks.
- Release at the earliest opportunity; comfort the child immediately after.

## 3.10 Paediatric pain assessment

| Scale | Age group | Method |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **FLACC** (Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability) | Pre-verbal, 0–3 years | Observer scores 0–2 each item; total 0–10 |
| **Wong-Baker FACES** | 3–8 years | Child points to the face that matches their pain; score 0–10 |
| **NRS** (Numeric Rating Scale) | ≥8 years | Child rates pain 0–10 verbally |

### Pain management

**Non-pharmacological**:
- **Sucrose (oral)** 0.5–2 mL of 24% sucrose 2 minutes before a procedure in neonates — reduces cry duration and FLACC score.
- Distraction (music, bubbles, story, holding a toy).
- **EMLA cream** (eutectic mixture of local anaesthetics) — apply 45–60 minutes before venepuncture under an occlusive dressing; reduces needle-insertion pain.
- Breastfeeding during the procedure in infants.

**Pharmacological**:
- **Paracetamol** 15 mg/kg orally every 4–6 hours for mild-moderate pain.
- **Ibuprofen** 5–10 mg/kg every 6–8 hours for mild-moderate pain (avoid < 3 months).
- **Morphine infusion** 20–40 mcg/kg/hour (titrated) for severe pain — requires careful monitoring of respiratory rate.

## 3.11 Informed consent and assent in paediatrics

- **Informed consent** must be obtained from a parent or legal guardian for any procedure or treatment.
- **Assent** — explaining the procedure in age-appropriate terms and asking for the child's agreement — should be sought from children old enough to understand (generally ≥7 years); it respects the child's developing autonomy even though it cannot replace parental consent.
- Document both consent and assent in the case record.

## Remember

- Toddlers suffer most from hospitalisation; the three phases of separation are Protest, Despair, Detachment.
- Rooming-in and parental presence reduce separation anxiety most effectively.
- Maintenance fluids: 100/50/20 rule (Holliday-Segar).
- IM injection in infants/toddlers: vastus lateralis.
- Confirm NG placement by aspiration (pH <5.5); X-ray if in doubt.
- Blood transfusion: 10–15 mL/kg packed red cells; complete within 4 hours.
- FLACC for pre-verbal, Faces for 3–8 years, NRS for ≥8 years.
- Sucrose 0.5–2 mL reduces procedural pain in neonates; EMLA cream 45 min before venepuncture.
- Informed consent from parent; assent from child ≥7 years.

# Unit 4: The healthy child — growth, development, nutrition and play

This unit covers INC Unit IV: normal growth and development from birth to adolescence, developmental screening, nutrition, common nutritional deficiencies, and the role of play. Growth and development milestones are examined very frequently — learn the table by heart.

---

## 4.1 Growth

**Growth** is an increase in physical size (weight, height, head circumference). It is the best single indicator of a child's health and nutrition.

### Weight

| Age | Expected weight |
| --- | --- |
| Birth | ~3 kg (2.5–3.5 kg) |
| 5 months | Doubles birth weight (~6 kg) |
| 1 year | Trebles birth weight (~9 kg) |
| 2 years | Quadruples birth weight (~12 kg) |
| 2–10 years | Gains ~2–3 kg per year |
| Puberty | Growth spurt (girls 10–14 years; boys 12–16 years) |

**Rule**: birth weight (kg) = age in months ÷ 2 + 4 (approximate, up to about 6 months).

### Length / Height

- Birth: ~50 cm
- 1 year: ~75 cm (adds ~25 cm in first year)
- 2 years: ~87 cm (adds ~12.5 cm in second year)
- 2–12 years: adds ~5–6 cm per year
- Puberty: adds 6–10 cm per year during the growth spurt

### Head circumference

- Birth: ~33–35 cm
- Months 1–3: adds ~2 cm per month
- Months 4–6: adds ~1 cm per month
- 1 year: ~47 cm
- 2 years: ~49–50 cm
- **Macrocephaly** (>+2 SD): hydrocephalus.
- **Microcephaly** (<−2 SD): congenital infection (TORCH), genetic syndromes.

### Fontanelles

- **Anterior fontanelle**: diamond-shaped, at junction of frontal and parietal bones. Closes **12–18 months**. Bulging fontanelle = raised intracranial pressure; sunken = dehydration.
- **Posterior fontanelle**: triangular, closes by **6–8 weeks**.

### Teeth

- 20 primary (deciduous) teeth: first tooth erupts at ~6 months (lower central incisors); all 20 by ~2.5 years.
- Permanent teeth begin at ~6 years.

### WHO child growth charts

WHO Child Growth Standards (released 2006) represent ideal growth under optimal conditions. Use Z-scores (standard deviations from the median):

| Indicator | Interpretation |
| --- | --- |
| Weight-for-age | Underweight (< −2 Z) |
| Length/height-for-age | Stunting (< −2 Z); reflects chronic malnutrition |
| Weight-for-length/height | Wasting (< −2 Z); reflects acute malnutrition |
| BMI-for-age | Overweight (> +2 Z) |
| MUAC < 11.5 cm | Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) |

## 4.2 Developmental domains and milestones

Childhood development is assessed across four domains:

1. **Gross motor** — large muscle movements (rolling, sitting, walking, running)
2. **Fine motor/adaptive** — small muscle movements, hand–eye coordination (reaching, pincer grip, drawing)
3. **Language/speech** — receptive (understanding) and expressive (speaking)
4. **Personal-social** — self-care, social interaction (smiling, feeding, dressing)

### Developmental milestones (birth to 5 years)

| Age | Gross motor | Fine motor | Language | Personal-social |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1 month** | Lifts chin prone | Hands fisted | Startles to sound | Regards face |
| **3 months** | Holds head steady; raises chest on arms | Opens hands; follows object 180° | Coos, vocalises | Social smile (key milestone) |
| **6 months** | Sits with support; rolls over | Palmar grasp; transfers objects hand to hand | Babbles; turns to voice | Recognises mother; stranger anxiety beginning |
| **9 months** | Sits without support; creeps/crawls | Inferior pincer grip | "Mama/dada" (non-specific) | Waves bye-bye; plays peek-a-boo |
| **12 months** | Stands alone; first steps | Mature pincer grip (finger + thumb) | 1–2 meaningful words | Stranger anxiety peak; cooperates with dressing |
| **18 months** | Walks well; runs stiffly | Stacks 2–3 cubes; scribbles | 10–20 words; uses cup | Feeds self with spoon; points to wants |
| **2 years** | Runs; walks up/down stairs with both feet per step | Stacks 6 cubes; copies vertical line | 2-word phrases; 50+ words | Parallel play; uses spoon and fork |
| **3 years** | Rides tricycle; stands on one foot for 3 s | Stacks 9–10 cubes; copies circle | 3-word sentences; 300 words; asks "why?" | Toilet trained day; dresses with help |
| **4 years** | Hops on one foot; climbs | Copies cross; holds pencil correctly | Full sentences; tells stories | Cooperative play; buttons; brushes teeth |
| **5 years** | Skips; jumps over rope | Copies triangle; draws person with 6 parts | Counts 10 objects; knows colours | Dresses independently; group play |

**Key milestones to memorise**:
- **Social smile**: 6–8 weeks (2 months)
- **Head control**: 3 months
- **Sitting without support**: 6–8 months
- **Pincer grip**: 9–12 months
- **Walking alone**: 12–15 months
- **Meaningful words**: 12 months
- **2-word phrases**: 2 years
- **Toilet training**: 2–3 years

## 4.3 Developmental red flags

Refer immediately if:
- Not smiling by 3 months
- Not sitting alone by 9 months
- Not walking by 18 months
- No speech by 18 months (not even babble)
- Loss of a previously acquired skill (**regression**) at any age — always abnormal and needs urgent investigation
- Not pointing to objects by 12 months (may indicate autism)
- M-CHAT-R (Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers) positive at 16–30 months

## 4.4 Developmental screening tools

| Tool | Age range | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Denver Developmental Screening Test II (DDST-II/DASII)** | 0–6 years | Screens gross motor, fine motor-adaptive, language, personal-social domains; 125 items |
| **Bayley Scales of Infant Development** | 1–42 months | Detailed assessment of motor, cognitive, language |
| **M-CHAT-R** | 16–30 months | Screening for autism; parent-completed questionnaire |
| **RBSK screening tool** | 0–18 years | Screens for 4 Ds at anganwadi and school level |

## 4.5 Developmental theories

| Theorist | Theory | Stages relevant to nursing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Erikson** (psychosocial) | Each stage has a central conflict; resolution builds personality | Infancy: Trust vs Mistrust; Toddler: Autonomy vs Shame/Doubt; Preschool: Initiative vs Guilt; School-age: Industry vs Inferiority; Adolescence: Identity vs Role Confusion |
| **Piaget** (cognitive) | Children build knowledge through interaction with the environment | Sensorimotor (0–2 y): learns through senses; Preoperational (2–7 y): magical thinking, egocentrism; Concrete Operational (7–11 y): logic about concrete objects; Formal Operational (11+ y): abstract thinking |
| **Freud** (psychosexual) | Personality forms through stages of sexual energy | Oral (infant), Anal (toddler), Phallic (3–6 y), Latency (6–12 y), Genital (12+) — less used clinically but useful context |

**Nursing application**: a toddler (Erikson: Autonomy) must be given limited choices during care ("Do you want your medicine now or after washing your face?") to maintain a sense of control.

## 4.6 Infant and young child nutrition

### Breastfeeding (0–6 months)

**Exclusive breastfeeding** means only breast milk — no water, no other milk, no food — for the first 6 months.

**Composition of breast milk**:
- **Foremilk** (first part of feed): watery, quenches thirst, lower fat.
- **Hindmilk** (last part): higher fat content; ensures caloric adequacy.
- **Colostrum** (first 3–5 days): thick, yellow, rich in IgA, lactoferrin, lymphocytes, macrophages; acts as the newborn's first immunisation.

**Immunological factors**: Secretory IgA (protects mucosal surfaces against pathogens), lactoferrin (bacteriostatic; binds iron away from bacteria), lysozyme, oligosaccharides (prebiotics), cytokines, macrophages. No formula replicates these.

**Signs of effective breastfeeding**: 8–12 feeds per day; at least 6–8 wet nappies per day; steady weight gain; baby appears satisfied; mother hears swallowing.

**Common breastfeeding problems**: engorgement (frequent feeding, warm compress), sore nipples (correct latch), insufficient milk (increase frequency, correct positioning), inverted nipple (breast shell).

### Complementary feeding (6–12 months)

- Introduce at 6 months (not before 4 months, not after 6 months).
- Start with soft pureed single-ingredient foods; gradually increase texture and variety.
- Introduce **iron-rich foods early** (fortified cereals, mashed lentils/dal, pureed meat).
- Introduce common allergens (egg, peanut) early (by 6–9 months) — delayed introduction increases allergy risk.
- **Avoid**: honey (risk of infant botulism), salt and sugar, whole nuts (choking), cow's milk as main drink before 1 year, low-fat dairy.

### Nutrition aged 1–5 years

- Family meals; a balanced diet with all food groups.
- Portion sizes are small — a child's portion ≈ one tablespoon per year of age.
- **5-a-day**: encourage five portions of fruit and vegetables daily.
- Iron-rich foods remain important; cow's milk should be limited to 350 mL/day (excessive milk displaces iron-rich foods).
- Calcium and vitamin D for bone growth; sunlight exposure.

## 4.7 Common nutritional deficiencies in India

### Iron-deficiency anaemia (IDA)

- Most common nutritional deficiency in Indian children.
- **Diagnosis**: Hb < 11 g/dL in children under 5 years; microcytic hypochromic red cells on smear; low serum ferritin.
- **Features**: pallor, fatigue, poor concentration, pica, irritability.
- **Treatment**: elemental iron **3–6 mg/kg/day** as ferrous sulfate or fumarate, divided 2–3 times daily, for **3 months** (minimum 6–8 weeks after Hb normalises to replenish stores); give between meals with vitamin C-rich juice (improves absorption); darkens stools — reassure parents.
- **Prevention**: iron-fortified foods, iron supplementation under NHM for children 6 months–5 years, deworming 2-yearly from 1 year.

### Vitamin A deficiency (VAD)

- **Causes**: poor dietary intake of beta-carotene (green leafy vegetables, yellow/orange fruits) or preformed vitamin A (liver, egg, dairy); aggravated by recurrent diarrhoea.
- **Features (xerophthalmia)**:
  - Night blindness (nyctalopia) — earliest sign
  - Bitot's spots (foamy white deposits on temporal conjunctiva)
  - Corneal xerosis → corneal ulceration → keratomalacia (liquefaction of the cornea) → blindness
- **Prevention/treatment**: mega-dose vitamin A supplementation on NIS — 1 lakh IU at 9 months, then 2 lakh IU every 6 months up to 5 years.
- Vitamin A is also given in acute measles and severe malnutrition.

### Iodine deficiency disorders (IDD)

- **Causes**: iodine-poor soil and water in hilly and flood-prone regions.
- **Effects**: in the foetus/neonate (cretinism — severe intellectual disability, deaf-mutism, hypothyroidism if the mother was iodine-deficient); in children and adults (goitre, hypothyroidism, impaired cognition).
- **Prevention**: universal iodisation of salt (India mandates ≥15 ppm iodine at consumer level); nurse's role: educate families to use iodised salt and store it in a covered container away from heat and light.

### Vitamin D deficiency rickets

- **Cause**: inadequate sunlight exposure, low dietary vitamin D, exclusive breastfeeding without D supplementation.
- **Features**: bow legs (genu varum), Harrison's sulcus (groove along lower rib margins), frontal bossing, craniotabes (softening of skull bones), delayed fontanelle closure, painful wrists with widened epiphyses (rachitic rosary), raised alkaline phosphatase, low serum calcium/phosphorus.
- **Treatment**: vitamin D **1,500–5,000 IU/day** orally for 3 months + calcium; then maintenance 400–1000 IU/day.
- **Prevention**: daily vitamin D 400 IU from birth for all breastfed infants; sunlight exposure.

## 4.8 Play

**Play is the primary occupation of childhood.** It promotes physical, cognitive, language, social-emotional, and creative development.

### Types of play (Parten's social categories)

| Type | Age | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Solitary play** | Infant–toddler | Plays alone with no interest in nearby children |
| **Parallel play** | Toddler (2–3 y) | Plays alongside other children with similar toys but no interaction — normal at this age |
| **Associative play** | Preschool (3–4 y) | Plays with others; shares materials but no organised goal |
| **Cooperative play** | School-age (4–6+ y) | Organised play with rules and a common goal |

### Age-appropriate toys

| Age | Suitable toys |
| --- | --- |
| Infant | Mobile over cot, rattles, soft toys, teething rings, face mirrors |
| Toddler | Stacking cups/rings, ride-on toys, push-pull toys, simple puzzles (3–4 pieces) |
| Preschool | Finger paints, play dough, role-play (dress-up, kitchen sets), larger puzzles |
| School-age | Board games, construction kits (Lego), team sports, craft materials, books |
| Adolescent | Team sports, music, art, crafts, age-appropriate video games |

**Safety**: no sharp edges; no small parts for < 3 years (choking risk); check age labels; supervise water and outdoor play.

## Remember

- Weight: doubles at 5 months, trebles at 1 year, quadruples at 2 years.
- Head circumference at 1 year ≈ 47 cm; anterior fontanelle closes 12–18 months.
- Key milestones: social smile 2 months; sits alone 6–8 months; walks alone 12–15 months; 2-word phrases 2 years.
- Red flag: **regression** (loss of a skill) is always abnormal.
- Exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months; complementary feeding from 6 months.
- IDA: Hb < 11 g/dL under 5 years; treatment elemental iron 3–6 mg/kg/day × 3 months.
- Vitamin A: night blindness → Bitot's spots → keratomalacia; NIS mega-dose at 9 months.
- Iodine deficiency → cretinism (maternal), goitre (child); prevent with iodised salt.
- Rickets: bow legs, Harrison's sulcus, raised ALP; treat with vitamin D + calcium.
- Parallel play is normal at 2–3 years; cooperative play from 4–5 years.

# Unit 5: Nursing care of the neonate — normal and high-risk

This unit covers INC Unit V: care of the normal newborn, assessment at birth, common conditions in the newborn period, and the special care needs of preterm, low-birth-weight, and other high-risk neonates. The Apgar score and neonatal jaundice management are very commonly examined.

---

## 5.1 The normal newborn — immediate care at birth

### Immediate steps (first 30 seconds)

1. **Warm and dry**: place the baby under a radiant warmer or on the mother's chest; dry thoroughly and remove wet linen (evaporation is the main cause of heat loss in the delivery room).
2. **Stimulate**: gentle drying and rubbing of the back.
3. **Airway**: if the baby is not breathing, suction mouth then nose with a bulb syringe or suction catheter (do not suction routinely).
4. **Assess**: breathing, heart rate, colour.
5. **Delayed cord clamping**: clamp and cut the umbilical cord at 1–3 minutes after birth (unless emergency requires earlier clamping); allows up to 80 mL extra blood to transfuse to the baby, reducing iron-deficiency anaemia risk.
6. **Skin-to-skin (Kangaroo Mother Care — KMC)**: place the naked baby prone on the mother's bare chest immediately; maintains temperature, promotes breastfeeding, stabilises heart rate and breathing.
7. **Initiate breastfeeding within 1 hour** of birth.

### Prophylaxis

- **Vitamin K 1 mg IM** into the anterolateral thigh — prevents haemorrhagic disease of the newborn (HDN; now called Vitamin K Deficiency Bleeding, VKDB).
- **Hepatitis B vaccine** (birth dose) within 24 hours.
- **BCG** and **OPV 0** at or soon after birth.
- **Eye prophylaxis**: 1% tetracycline or 0.5% erythromycin ointment into both eyes prevents gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum.

## 5.2 Apgar score

Assessed at **1 minute** and **5 minutes** after birth. Each of 5 signs is scored 0, 1, or 2.

| Sign | 0 | 1 | 2 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **A**ppearance (colour) | Blue/pale all over | Blue extremities, pink body | Completely pink |
| **P**ulse (heart rate) | Absent | < 100 /min | ≥ 100 /min |
| **G**rimace (reflex irritability) | No response to stimulation | Grimace | Cry, cough, or sneeze |
| **A**ctivity (muscle tone) | Limp | Some flexion | Active motion |
| **R**espiration | Absent | Weak/irregular | Strong cry |

**Interpretation**:
- **7–10**: normal; routine care.
- **4–6**: moderate depression; stimulate, give supplemental O₂, may need brief PPV.
- **0–3**: severe depression; begin neonatal resuscitation immediately.

The 5-minute Apgar is more prognostically important. A score < 7 at 5 minutes → rescore at 10, 15, and 20 minutes.

## 5.3 Normal newborn assessment

**Vital signs**: Temperature 36.5–37.5°C, HR 120–160/min, RR 40–60/min.

**Weight**: 2.5–4.0 kg; physiological weight loss of 7–10% in first 3–4 days (then regains birth weight by 10–14 days); gain ~20–30 g/day thereafter.

**Systematic examination**: head (fontanelles, caput succedaneum vs cephalhaematoma), eyes (red reflex, discharge), ears (shape, position), mouth (cleft, Epstein pearls), neck (clavicle fracture), chest (breast engorgement — normal), abdomen (cord, organomegaly), genitalia (undescended testes in males, ambiguous genitalia), anus (patency), limbs (talipes, polydactyly, single palmar crease — trisomy 21), spine (neural tube defects), skin (milia, erythema toxicum, Mongolian blue spot — normal).

**Gestational age assessment (Ballard Score)**: combines neuromuscular maturity (posture, square window, arm recoil, popliteal angle, scarf sign, heel-to-ear) and physical maturity (skin, lanugo, plantar creases, breast, eye/ear, genitalia). Score correlates with gestational age in weeks (20–44 weeks).

## 5.4 Common conditions in the newborn

### Neonatal jaundice

**Physiological jaundice** (normal):
- Appears **after 24 hours** of life.
- Peaks at day 3–5.
- Disappears by day 10–14 in term infants (can extend to 3 weeks in breastfed infants).
- Due to: high RBC turnover, immature liver, enterohepatic recirculation.
- Assess by **Kramer's zones** (progressive cephalocaudal spread of jaundice):

```text
Zone 1: face/neck     — Bilirubin ~5 mg/dL
Zone 2: trunk         — ~10 mg/dL
Zone 3: below navel   — ~12 mg/dL
Zone 4: arms/legs     — ~15 mg/dL
Zone 5: palms/soles   — >15 mg/dL
```

Confirm with serum total bilirubin (STB) measurement; use the Bhutani nomogram for gestational age-specific thresholds.

**Pathological jaundice** — suspect if:
- Appears **within 24 hours** of birth.
- Rising bilirubin > 0.5 mg/dL/hour.
- STB exceeds the phototherapy threshold for the baby's gestation and age in hours.
- **Direct (conjugated) bilirubin** > 2 mg/dL.
- Persists beyond 2 weeks (term) or 3 weeks (preterm).

**Causes of pathological jaundice**: Rh incompatibility (anti-D), ABO incompatibility (anti-A, anti-B), G6PD deficiency, sepsis, congenital hypothyroidism, biliary atresia (conjugated).

### Phototherapy

**Indications**: STB at or approaching the phototherapy threshold for gestation and age (use hospital nomogram/NNF/WHO guidelines).

**Mechanism**: blue-green light (420–490 nm) converts bilirubin in the skin to water-soluble photoisomers excreted in bile and urine without conjugation.

**Nursing care during phototherapy**:
- Place baby under phototherapy lights at the correct distance (typically 25–30 cm for conventional fluorescent; manufacturer-specified for LED/blanket types).
- **Cover eyes** with phototherapy eye mask (patches) — prevents retinal damage; check every 2 hours; remove briefly for feeds.
- **Keep genitalia covered** in male infants (theoretical gonadal risk).
- Keep baby unclothed (maximum skin exposure) except for the nappy.
- Increase fluid intake (additional 10–20% of feeds) — phototherapy increases insensible fluid loss.
- Monitor temperature: phototherapy lamps generate heat — check temperature 4-hourly.
- Document light position, eye patch, feeds, urine output, bilirubin levels.
- Rebound bilirubin check 12–24 hours after stopping phototherapy.

**Exchange transfusion** (double volume): indicated when STB exceeds the exchange transfusion threshold or if there is acute bilirubin encephalopathy (poor feeding, high-pitched cry, opisthotonus, seizures). Replaces sensitised/haemolysed red cells and removes bilirubin.

### Neonatal sepsis

- **Early-onset** (< 72 hours): usually maternal organisms (GBS, E. coli, Listeria); risk factors: prolonged rupture of membranes > 18 h, maternal fever, chorioamnionitis, GBS colonisation.
- **Late-onset** (> 72 hours): hospital-acquired organisms (Klebsiella, Staph. aureus, Pseudomonas) or community organisms; risk factors: prematurity, IV lines, TPN.
- **Features**: temperature instability (hypothermia more common than fever in neonates), poor feeding/sucking, lethargy, apnoea, respiratory distress, bulging fontanelle (meningitis), jaundice, abdominal distension.
- **Management**: blood culture before antibiotics, then IV ampicillin + gentamicin (early onset) or IV cefotaxime + vancomycin if hospital-acquired; supportive care.

### Other common newborn conditions

- **Neonatal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum)**: mucopurulent discharge within 28 days; gonococcal (1–3 days) is an emergency; chlamydial (5–14 days). Culture and treat; prophylaxis with antibiotic eye ointment.
- **Oral thrush (candidiasis)**: white plaques on buccal mucosa that cannot be wiped off; treat with oral nystatin suspension 100,000 units after feeds, 4 times daily.
- **Umbilical cord care**: keep dry; wipe with clean water; sign of infection — redness, discharge, smell → umbilical sepsis → IV antibiotics; omphalitis can extend to portal vein thrombosis.

## 5.5 High-risk neonate — preterm infant

**Preterm**: < 37 completed weeks gestational age.

### Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS / Hyaline Membrane Disease)

- **Cause**: surfactant deficiency (surfactant is produced from ~24 weeks; adequate amounts by 35–36 weeks).
- **Features**: tachypnoea, grunting, nasal flaring, subcostal/sternal retractions, cyanosis — worsening in the first 24–48 hours; CXR shows "ground glass" opacity with air bronchograms.
- **Management**:
  - Antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone to mother at 24–34 weeks) accelerate surfactant production.
  - After birth: **surfactant therapy** (intratracheal) reduces severity and mortality; CPAP to maintain alveolar patency; mechanical ventilation if severe.
  - Nurse: monitor SpO₂ and blood gases, titrate O₂ carefully (avoid hyperoxia → retinopathy), maintain temperature, provide expressed breast milk feeds by NG.

### Other major prematurity complications

- **Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP)**: abnormal retinal vascularisation due to oxygen toxicity; screen all infants < 32 weeks or < 1500 g at 4–6 weeks of age; treat severe ROP with laser photocoagulation or anti-VEGF injection.
- **Intraventricular haemorrhage (IVH)**: bleeding into the germinal matrix → ventricles; most common in < 32 weeks; graded I–IV; Grade III–IV → hydrocephalus, neurodevelopmental delay.
- **Necrotising enterocolitis (NEC)**: ischaemic/infectious bowel necrosis; features: abdominal distension, bloody stools, feed intolerance, air in bowel wall (pneumatosis intestinalis on X-ray); treatment: bowel rest (nil by mouth), IV antibiotics, surgical resection if perforation.
- **Apnoea of prematurity**: cessation of breathing > 20 seconds with bradycardia and desaturation; treat with caffeine citrate (stimulates respiratory centre).

### Incubator (isolette) care for preterm infants

- Closed incubator maintains temperature (thermoneutral environment 32–36°C depending on weight/gestation), humidity (60–80%), and reduces infection.
- Minimal handling to avoid desaturation episodes; developmental positioning (facilitated tucking, nesting rolls).
- Expressed breast milk through NG tube; advance feeds slowly to reduce NEC risk.

## 5.6 Low-birth-weight, IUGR and post-term neonates

| Category | Definition | Key concerns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LBW | Birth weight < 2500 g | Hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, infection, poor feeding |
| VLBW | Birth weight < 1500 g | All the above plus RDS, IVH, NEC, ROP |
| IUGR — symmetric | Both weight and length reduced; insult from early pregnancy (TORCH infections, chromosomal) | Neurodevelopmental delay, difficulty with catch-up growth |
| IUGR — asymmetric | Weight reduced, length normal; insult in late pregnancy (placental insufficiency, hypertension) | Polycythaemia, hypoglycaemia, fetal distress in labour |
| Post-term | > 42 weeks | Meconium aspiration syndrome, hypoglycaemia, polycythaemia |

**Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC)** for LBW: skin-to-skin contact between mother and baby 24 hours a day; replaces incubator in stable LBW infants > 1500 g; reduces hypothermia, infection, mortality, promotes breastfeeding.

## 5.7 Birth asphyxia — neonatal resuscitation (NRP)

Approximately 10% of newborns need some assistance at birth; 1% need extensive resuscitation.

```text
NRP Algorithm:
   Baby born → Assess (term? breathing? good tone?)
      YES to all → Routine care (warmth, airway, dry, skin-to-skin)
      NO to any →
         → Warm, dry, stimulate, suction if secretions visible
         → Assess breathing and HR at 30 s
         If HR < 100 or apnoeic → PPV with 21% O₂ (room air)
         → Assess at 60 s
         If HR < 100 → Check technique, consider O₂ increase
         If HR < 60 → Start chest compressions (3:1 with PPV)
         If HR < 60 persists → Intubate, IV/IO adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg
```

**Key points**:
- Start PPV with 21% O₂ (room air); increase only if SpO₂ not improving.
- Compressions: 2-thumb encircling technique; depth 1/3 AP diameter; rate 90 compressions + 30 breaths per minute.
- Adrenaline: 0.01–0.03 mg/kg IV/IO; 0.05–0.1 mg/kg via ETT (less effective).

## 5.8 Neonatal hypoglycaemia and hypothermia

### Hypoglycaemia

- **Definition**: blood glucose < 2.6 mmol/L (< 47 mg/dL) in a neonate.
- **At-risk groups**: LBW, preterm, IDM (infant of diabetic mother — macrosomic), IUGR, stressed infants.
- **Features**: jitteriness, poor feeding, hypotonia, apnoea, seizures; often asymptomatic.
- **Treatment**: if symptomatic or glucose persistently < 2.6 mmol/L — 2 mL/kg of 10% dextrose IV as a bolus over 5 minutes; then infuse GIR 6–8 mg/kg/min; recheck glucose 30 minutes later.
- **Prevention**: early and frequent feeds; monitor blood glucose in at-risk infants at 1, 3, and 6 hours.

### Hypothermia

- **Normal neonatal temperature**: 36.5–37.5°C.
- **Cold stress (mild hypothermia)**: 36.0–36.5°C — increases oxygen consumption and glucose use; increases apnoea.
- **Hypothermia** < 36°C — increases mortality, especially in LBW.
- **Causes**: cold delivery room, delayed drying and dressing, bathing too soon.
- **Chain of warmth**: warm delivery room (> 25°C), immediate drying, skin-to-skin or radiant warmer, delayed first bath (after 24 hours or once temperature stable), warm transport.
- **Thermoneutral environment**: in an incubator, the temperature at which the baby requires minimal oxygen to maintain a normal core temperature.

## 5.9 Congenital abnormalities

| Condition | Key nursing points |
| --- | --- |
| **CHD — cyanotic** (Tetralogy of Fallot, TGA) | SpO₂ monitoring; prostaglandin E₁ to maintain PDA for duct-dependent lesions; prepare for surgery |
| **CHD — acyanotic** (VSD, ASD, PDA) | Monitor for heart failure (poor feeding, tachycardia, hepatomegaly); diuretics; surgery/catheter |
| **Cleft lip/palate** | Special feeding (squeezable bottle, Haberman feeder); surgery for cleft lip at ~3 months, palate at ~9–12 months; speech therapy; support parents |
| **Neural tube defects — spina bifida** | Cover the sac with sterile saline-soaked gauze; prevent infection; catheterise if bladder retention; surgical closure within 24–48 hours |
| **Talipes equinovarus (club foot)** | Ponseti method: serial plaster casting from birth changing every 5–7 days for 6–8 weeks; followed by percutaneous Achilles tenotomy; then foot abduction brace (Mitchell brace) for 3 years |

## Remember

- Immediate care at birth: Warm, Dry, Stimulate, Suction (if needed), Delayed cord clamping 1–3 min.
- Vitamin K 1 mg IM at birth prevents HDN.
- Apgar: score each of 5 signs 0–2 at 1 and 5 minutes; 7–10 normal, 4–6 moderate, 0–3 severe.
- Physiological jaundice: appears > 24 hours, peaks day 3–5, clears by day 10–14.
- Pathological jaundice: appears < 24 hours or bilirubin rising rapidly — investigate.
- Phototherapy: eye patches, unclothed, increase fluids, check temperature.
- Neonatal sepsis: temperature instability, poor feeding, lethargy — blood culture before antibiotics.
- Preterm: RDS (surfactant deficiency), ROP (O₂ toxicity), IVH, NEC, apnoea.
- KMC for stable LBW > 1500 g: 24-hour skin-to-skin, reduces mortality.
- Neonatal hypoglycaemia (< 2.6 mmol/L): early feeds; treat symptomatic with 2 mL/kg 10% dextrose IV.
- Cleft lip surgery ~3 months, cleft palate ~9–12 months.
- Club foot (talipes): Ponseti serial casting then Mitchell brace.
